item.title: The Tall Poppy Problem: Why Excellence Often Faces Backlash
item.description:
Jealousy

The Tall Poppy Problem: Why Excellence Often Faces Backlash

How organizations can punish both ethical and exceptional employees.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Envy compares visible surfaces, often mistaking others’ success for undeserved advantage.
  • Rising, ethical, high-performing people can become “tall poppies” targeted for standing out.
  • Threatened leaders can weaponize hierarchies to remove productive subordinates and effectively stop reformers.

Envy may be humanity’s oldest flaw.

In the Judeo-Christian creation story, Cain kills Abel after God favors Abel’s offering. Whether or not one reads the story literally, it captures something psychologically ancient: the pain of seeing another person receive what we want, and the temptation to remove the person who makes us feel inferior.

That force is still with us. There is good evidence that our happiness depends not only on what we have, but on how we compare with those around us. Economists have repeatedly found that subjective well-being is affected by relative income and status, not simply by absolute levels of wealth.

But comparison has a fundamental flaw: we compare surfaces. We see the promotion, not the years of rejection. The prospering family, not the private health struggles. The wealth, not the sacrifices behind it. The privilege, not the difficult childhood. We compare what is visible about someone else with what we know about ourselves. So what happens when comparison turns into envy?

Envy can be productive—or destructive

An upward comparison can motivate us: I want what she has, so I will work to become better. But envy can also take the opposite route: If I cannot have what she has, I want her to have less of it. Psychologists distinguish between benign envy, which can motivate self-improvement, and malicious envy, which can lead people to undermine the person they envy.

And this is where organizations become particularly interesting.

Envy can punish excellence

Source: Laura M Goodsell/Unsplash

The evidence that envy can target excellence is unusually strong. A multi-source three-wave lagged field study of supervisors and subordinates found that high subordinate performance is linked to supervisory undermining, consistent with an envy-mediated pathway from subordinate performance to abusive supervision, among supervisors high in social-comparison orientation.

The “tall poppy” literature points in the same direction. In Feather’s experimental studies, people reported greater pleasure when a high achiever failed than when an average achiever failed.

Research on social comparison also suggests that people can be threatened not only by those already above them, but by colleagues who are rising faster than they are. In other words, you do not necessarily have to be at the top to become threatening. It may be enough to be on your way there. This creates a disturbing organizational possibility: a workplace can end up punishing precisely the people it most needs.

Don't shine too brightly. Don't rise too quickly. Don't make your boss look bad.

Envy is not always about performance

There is another, perhaps even more important, dimension: ethics.

In four experiments published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Monin, Sawyer, and Marquez found that people who themselves participated in objectionable conduct could dislike a person who refused to participate on principle. The rejection was mediated by the perception that the moral rebel implicitly condemned those who complied.

The target does not have to say, You are doing something wrong. Their behavior can communicate it anyway. This may be particularly relevant to whistleblowers, employees who refuse unethical practices, and people who visibly adhere to standards that others violate.

When reform threatens the people who must implement it

Now imagine a bold reformer entering an organization. A new government arrives with a clear anti-corruption mandate. A new CEO announces a restructuring. A new leader promises to reward performance, improve accountability, or eliminate entrenched privileges.

The reformer arrives with good intentions.

But the reformer usually takes the existing formal hierarchy as good and given. And they cannot see the invisible structure underneath it. They may not know who is corrupt and who is honest within a ministry. They may not know which manager will be inspired by an excellent subordinate and which will feel threatened by her. They may not know who has the self-confidence to welcome a rising colleague—and who needs to keep potential competitors safely below them, or better: kick them out.

Source: Dmytro Koplyk/Unsplash

Meanwhile, everyone inside the organization knows.

The masks are well rehearsed. A Potemkin village can be remarkably convincing when the president, CEO, or minister comes to visit.

And this is where well-intentioned reform can produce the opposite of what it intended.

If reform leaves the existing hierarchy largely intact, threatened managers can use that hierarchy to defend themselves. A corrupt boss may marginalize the ethical subordinate who refuses to go along. An insecure or unproductive boss may undermine the proactive subordinate who makes their own limitations apparent.

A threatened manager may remove the most formidable potential competitor—not because that person is doing anything wrong, but because she is becoming too good, too visible, or too difficult to control.

Meanwhile, the reformer thinks they are changing the system. The system may instead be using its existing people and incentives to neutralize the reform. The moat gets built so no rival reaches the castle.

When envy becomes an organizational force

This is why reform cannot be only about policies, structures and formal incentives. It also has to understand the psychology of the people who will implement them.

A good policy in the hands of someone whose status, power, or self-image it threatens can become something very different from what its designer intended. And this is where envy becomes more than an unpleasant human emotion. It can become an organizational force.

A statically governed organization may create a strange equilibrium in which being exceptional carries an interpersonal cost. People learn, consciously or unconsciously, not to stand out too much. And those who do may find themselves subtly isolated, undermined or cut down.

And here we return to Cain and Abel. If envy is indeed one of humanity’s oldest destructive forces, organizations cannot simply hope that it will disappear. They need ways to protect the people who stand out—and to let those who see what is happening reach the person with the power to act.

Source: Ayush Design/Unsplash

In practice, that may mean giving tall poppies—and those who see them being cut down—a direct, trusted channel to the reformer, or their closest advisers. Because sometimes the most important protection against dysfunction is not another rule. It is a hotline.

item.title: 3 Grief Triggers That Can Catch You Off Guard
item.description:
Grief

3 Grief Triggers That Can Catch You Off Guard

Grief is an inevitable part of life. Here’s what to know when it strikes.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Everyone experiences loss; grief reminds us we are human.
  • As hard as grieving may be, we can learn to expect triggers—even when unexpected.
  • Taking a moment to acknowledge grief can help heal it a bit, rather than letting it build and fester.
Source: Karola G/Pexels

When loss is fresh, you might not even imagine a time when you won’t grab your phone before remembering the person you want to call is no longer alive. Your brain takes months to grasp someone has died; your neurons have to physically reconfigure until they “know” this person no longer walks the earth and can’t be contacted (in customary ways, that is; it’s possible to create what we call continuing bonds following a death).

In time, you might feel guilty for laughing, enjoying friends, and progressing with romance, work, parenting, or a social life. You move ahead and that’s how it should be—there is no cause for guilt; healthy grieving involves re-embracing life. And your loved one, in any healthy relationship, would wish that for you.

But grief comes in waves and whether it’s an anniversary, birthday, a new loss, or even a friend experiencing grief, those waves may hit. Maybe it’s not a wave, but a tsunami, crashing into you until you’re laid out, calling in sick, clutching a loved one’s unwashed T-shirt, even years later. What just happened?

Although grief is universal, it’s also unpredictable and capricious—sudden, unbidden, surprising. It doesn’t arrive only when wanted; those waves hit no matter what the weather report foretold.

When grief blows by, it’s helpful to let it. If you’re with others, excuse yourself and find a place to breathe, walk around, or sit quietly with some favorite music. Grief can’t hurt you (or at least not in any way cold water on the face can’t fix). Taking even a quick moment to acknowledge the knife-edge of pain or the jagged breath that doesn’t seem to release, naming it as grief, and letting it wash over you may be all that’s needed before tackling the next thing. Shoving it away and avoiding it, though, simply adds to a bigger cavern inside.

3 Common Grief Triggers

After returning to life, those who are grieving can be taken aback by waves they didn’t expect. We call these triggers, and while anything random can trigger grief, here are three common ones. Just expecting the unexpected (rather than being completely surprised) and knowing triggers are universal can help you ride—and survive—the waves.

  1. Grief “anniversaries” don’t just mean the date you met or married. They can mean the anniversary of getting that life-changing diagnosis, a birthday, the date of death, the last time your loved one was able to do something special together, favorite holidays, or anything else. Awareness helps, and preparing for a grief anniversary can be even better. Write a letter to your dead loved one. Take a mental health day and drive to the beach or forest. Have dinner with mutual friends. Light a candle or visit a sanctuary. Play reminiscent music or read their favorite author. Whatever you do doesn’t matter, as long as it has meaning for you. In time, grief anniversaries may be a welcome time to honor and reminisce or share memories with family or friends, marking how important your loved one’s presence was in your life.
  2. Random triggers are, by definition, random. Keep that in mind. Maybe your best friend’s dad just got diagnosed with the disease your loved one had. Perhaps you’re driving by a bakery advertising your loved one’s favorite, off-brand donut. Maybe it’s the scent of someone’s perfume, their favorite plant or flower; a show, podcast, or voice. It could be a stranger walking through a crowd who you think, for a split second, is them, alive. Possibilities are infinite, and that’s okay. These are reminders to take a moment and remember you are grieving, and that’s expected. Share the moment with someone who understands, or simply acknowledge “grief,” “missing,” “longing” to yourself. You’ll know when it’s time to move on.
  3. Compound loss and compound grief are real, maybe inevitable. New griefs pile on old. It’s inevitable we lose people, pets, and so on. Someday, we will be the one who dies. That’s hard for humans to comprehend, and every new grief can compound the old ones, especially if we haven’t processed or acknowledged past griefs fully. Even if we have, grief can hit anew for a long-gone loss when we lose someone recent. Just knowing compound loss is real can help healing.

In all these ways grief can find us when expected, and even when not. Without it, we wouldn’t be human. But there’s one important caveat: if grief is unrelenting and keeping you from engaging in life again or even functioning, it’s time to get help. You may be grieving, but you’re alive and deserve to live. Reach out, nationally or locally, and begin life again.

Source: Ivan S/Pexels

item.title: Neurodiversity, Human Experience, and the Hiring Machine
item.description:
Neurodiversity

Neurodiversity, Human Experience, and the Hiring Machine

Automated hiring systems may perpetuate exclusion instead of progress.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Biased hiring practices can be magnified and scaled by technology.
  • Using data collected in unfair systems to train algorithmic selection codifies bias.
  • Fairness in hiring must start with humans designing and establishing fairer systems, not with automation.
A small beige kitchen.
Source: Lisa Anna/Pexels

Applying for jobs is stressful for most people. And it does not help when you know that "people like you" are likely to have a gigantic minus placed on their application—increasingly, by a machine.

The automated screening process is frequently met with applicant suspicion (1, 2). And in many cases, for good reason—the process is indeed fraught with bias. As just one example, older applicants are now given advice on outsmarting ageist bias, which appears to be built into many automated applicant screening systems and AI-saturated hiring models, by removing or condensing information on earlier experience and education (2). Sadly, even if removing older positions will help one person get a job, it does nothing to address ageism. If anything, it further embeds the connection between “too much experience" and "unhireable” into the system—and the cycle of ageism continues.

The cycle of biased practices begetting more biased practices can be clearly illustrated by analyzing neuroexclusion at work.

Neurodivergence, measurement validity, and the irony of human bias

Many automated screening systems reproduce biases that exist in manual resume screening. However, expanded versions of automated screening may include additional barriers traceable to the lack of validity—the correspondence between measurement and what is supposedly being measured. One of the validity challenges here is that systems with built-in assessments, such as personality testing, are rarely validated for neurodivergent candidates. Another issue is that these assessments may also not sufficiently correspond to the specific position and what is required for performance (3).

Of course, negative assumptions about neurodivergent people were prevalent long before the widespread use of automated screening. Yet, the world of human bias also presented some workarounds that, ironically, could allow for a more valid assessment of actual ability than "official" systems. Consider Temple Grandin, the famous autistic author and professor. For much of her early career, she used portfolios of her work to impress hiring managers and sidestep the likely discrimination based on her autistic differences (4). But at that time, Temple Grandin was not dealing with automated screening systems and could show her drawings and photos of completed projects to hiring managers. Would she have made it through and been able to show her portfolio in today’s world? Or would she have been automatically screened out?

When bias is located in a human, it can be corrected locally. When bias is located in the black box of algorithmic screening provided by monopoly vendors to a large number of employers, the potential to harm rises exponentially.

Data-based is not the same as fair

Most automated systems are trained on data that historically predicted employee success. But data-based is not the same as fair: data quality and the way it was collected matter. Because of the long-term exclusion, current applicant screening systems are not trained on neurodivergent employee data. They are also not trained on data that would apply to neuroinclusive environments. The impact of long-standing exclusion on data used to predict success is a fairness concern that may take a long time to address.

Again, the role of bad data in exclusion is best understood as a cycle. Organizational practices that keep neurodivergent people out of work may contribute to a lack of information on whether existing screening and selection procedures are valid and can accurately predict their success in the workplace. In turn, the lack of screening approaches validated for neurodivergent populations may perpetuate unemployment. The cycle closes.

Here’s an example of what happens when we use typically available data to train automated systems. Imagine that we are predicting the success of individuals in doing cooking tasks. We give them all an opportunity to cook in a kitchen and measure their speed and accuracy in the food prep. Sounds fair, right? On further examination, let’s say the kitchen is built for people who are around 5½ feet (168 cm) tall with no disabilities. We use that same kitchen to test the success of everyone: average-height people, those who are 4 feet tall, those who are 7 feet tall, and wheelchair users. Although the people who do not “fit” the kitchen show incredible ingenuity to accomplish their task, their success requires extra time and effort. Very few pass the test and are hired. Even fewer become master chefs. Over time, we have enough data to justify that being 5½ feet tall is a valid predictor of an aspiring chef’s success. Which it is, but only because the kitchen is built for these people.

Should we continue hiring 5½-foot-tall chefs, allowing the automated screening to exclude applicants who don’t meet the height requirement because it is technically “predictive”? Or should we make kitchens more flexible and accessible to avoid automatically screening out a wider pool of applicants?

By the same logic, what makes more sense: Should organizations continue to exclude neurodivergent people based on the data collected in exclusionary environments? Or should we make organizations neuroinclusive and collect better data? Algorithmic selection won't make hiring more just unless human justice comes first.

If we don’t break the cycle of using prior unfairness to excuse present and future unfairness, our data and technology serve to make entrenched biases even more entrenched. That hardly qualifies as progress. But designing systems for human dignity that integrate the best of appropriately used technology and the best of human judgment, has the potential to support both progress and fairness.

This post is an edited excerpt from my book, The Canary Code: A Guide to Neurodiversity, Dignity, and Intersectional Belonging at Work. A shorter version also appeared in the Best Work for Your Brain newsletter.

item.title: Do You Fawn?
item.description:
Boundaries

Do You Fawn?

How appeasing others can erode self-respect and personal boundaries.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Fawning is a way trauma survivors keep themselves safe.
  • I know I'm fawning when I feel small and acquiesce to another's interests.
  • Learning how to unfawn honors my integrity and deepens my relationships.
Source: Robert Woeger/Unsplash

On a recent road trip, my partner and I decided to listen to an audiobook. The first title that popped up was Fawning: Why the Need to Please Makes Us Lose Ourselves and How to Find Our Way Back. Over the course of the next several hundred miles, we found ourselves nodding, pausing the narration, and discussing how we each exhibit fawning behavior.

Written by a fellow Psychology Today blogger, Dr. Ingrid Clayton’s posts have attracted over 1 million views. Now that I’m primed to recognize what fawning looks like, such readership is no surprise. Most everyone I know fawns at least a bit. I fear I fawn more than many.

Fawning is the fourth “F” in how we respond to perceived threats—fight, flight, freeze, and fawn. Defined by psychotherapist Pete Walker as “a response to threat by becoming more appealing to the threat," internally it feels like I’m making myself small.

Although I’m quite a bit taller than the average woman and was once referred to as “formidable” by an old online dating prospect, I often feel quite small. I grew up in an emotionally and physically abusive household, where my efforts at fighting, fleeing, or freezing resulted in painful outcomes from my caregivers.

It wasn’t until I was an adult that I realized I could defuse conflict and protect myself by accommodating others’ interests at the expense of my own. I see now the steep price of keeping the peace.

By fawning, I seemed to derive positive regard from others. While fawning seemed to work in budding romantic relationships, I soon lost sight of my own needs. Pleasing others gradually became second nature to me at home, at school, and at work. As I ran myself ragged fulfilling others’ wants, I lost my voice and chipped away at my backbone.

My fawning reached its acme during divorce negotiations over a decade ago. While I hoped for an amicable settlement based on our respective circumstances, I almost acquiesced to a lopsided property agreement. I got scared and took a few days to regroup. Thanks to the support of a friend with financial chops, I soon presented my ex with my best and final offer, which pencilled out better for me and impacted him only minimally. Then I stopped talking and simply waited.

Source: Lucas Kaufmann/Pixabay

In those long moments of silence, I could almost feel my backbone regenerating itself. I breathed deeply and rested in the quiet space. I did not feel small. Instead I found my integrity, along with a side of grit I’d surrendered to fawning. I’m proud to say I prevailed.

Today I’m in a years-long partnership founded on a commitment to honesty and mutual respect. Though our fawning styles are different, each of us is learning to identify and revise our own behaviors. Every time I articulate my needs I feel less anxious afterwards. When I resort to fawning, I soon catch myself, take a deep breath, and try again.

item.title: What You Should Know About Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy
item.description:
Traumatic Brain Injury

What You Should Know About Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy

The neurodegeneration may be recognized early, leading to prompt intervention.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Chronic traumatic encephalopathy is a neurodegenerative disease correlated with collision sports.
  • CTE has an insidious onset, evolving into four stages, from mild mood changes to Alzheimer's-like dementia.
  • It can only be diagnosed post-mortem but can be suspected in athletes based on symptoms and sport history.
  • There is no cure, but CTE-type symptoms can be treated, making screening for potential CTE cases essential.
Source: Chris Chow/Unsplash

A perusal of the recent news will reveal headlines pertaining to football players’ brain trauma and a corollary degenerative brain disease called chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE. CTE is highly correlated with collision sports, particularly football and boxing, where athletes are most prone to numerous head-jarring impacts. It may sound familiar because it made the news in 2017 when researchers examined the brain of former New England Patriots player Aaron Hernandez. Convicted of murder and serving a life sentence, Hernandez died by suicide and his brain was donated to Boston University’s CTE Center.

Researchers at Boston University reported to the press that they found Hernandez’s CTE to be the worst case they had seen in a young individual (Barlow, 2019). As an aside, no one has ever singled out CTE as the cause of Hernandez’s criminal behavior, as he had a complicated early family dynamic and significant substance abuse history, both of which shape one’s personality and behaviors.

Neurodegenerative dynamics of CTE

The condition is known to cause significant dysfunction in the amygdala, hippocampus and thalamus—brain regions that support memory, emotion and behavior (John et al., 2025). The frontal lobes, which are involved in numerous cognitive processes including attention and executive functioning, are also affected (McKee at al., 2013).

CTE made the news most recently because it was reported in the British Medical Journal (Daneshvar, August 2026) that one in four former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021, a period when brain donation was most frequent, showed CTE upon examination. What is more alarming is that the researchers reported it is likely more common. As a progressive disease, it may silently creep for years, feasibly beginning in youth and college collision sports players. Famed CTE researcher Dr. Ann McKee stated that a study she did in 2023, “…clearly shows that the pathology of CTE starts early…The fact that over 40% of young contact and collision sport athletes in the UNITE Brain Bank have CTE is remarkable” (Doctrow, 2023). It was also noted that, at the time, the youngest person ever diagnosed with it was 17.

While collision sport athletes are at a higher risk for CTE, clearly not everyone develops it. One reason may be that people with CTE also had genetic mutations like those found in Alzheimer’s disease (Dong et al., 2025). Perhaps there is a biological predisposition instigated by repeated head traumas. Regardless, the correlation between repetitive head jarring and CTE is uncanny, and protecting athletes’ heads has become a hot topic once again.

Many parents may be left wondering if they should allow their child to continue to play football, and college and professional athletes might be questioning their careers. Helmets help but merely absorb the shock; the head still gets jarred. Is one’s current athleticism setting them up for later-in-life neurodegenerative conditions, even as soon as their late teens or 20s?

How is CTE officially diagnosed?

Unfortunately, CTE cannot be officially diagnosed until a postmortem examination of the brain, because brain tissue must be examined for tau protein, something that is linked to neurodegeneration. While imaging studies might show brain damage, it is the link to tau protein that makes CTE unique, similar to how amyloid plaque is correlated to Alzheimer’s (e.g. Katsumoto et al., 2019). Ideally, researchers will eventually be able to examine the brain tissue of living subjects with symptoms and discover how to control its presence or expansion.

Can doctors suspect CTE and provide intervention?

In the meantime, doctors can suspect CTE based on symptoms and sport history. While there is not yet a cure, there is evidence that athletes with suspected CTE can be treated with medication and lifestyle changes (e.g. Rossi, 2023). NFL players have been made more aware of this after the recent Daneshvar et al. study. Quoting from a letter shared by NBC Sports that the NFL Player’s Union sent out to players:

According to Dr. Daniel Daneshvar, one of the lead researchers on the study, ‘Many of the symptoms associated with CTE are treatable with the right care.’ He stressed that, ‘While we don’t have a cure yet, we have seen improvements in players who receive care from doctors specializing in neurodegenerative disease and who know how to treat athletes. No one should walk away thinking there’s nothing they can do.'

With that in mind, recognizing possible signs of CTE is an important first step. According to Fesharaki-Zadeh (2019), there are four stages of CTE, each with their respective presentation, as follows:

Source: Cottonbro/Pexels
  1. The person is asymptomatic or may exhibit mild short-term memory deficits and/or depressive symptoms.
  2. Mood and behavioral symptoms like aggressive outbursts and/or more severe depressive symptoms can appear.
  3. This stage is marked by more cognitive symptoms such as further memory loss, impaired executive functioning, visuospatial dysfunction, and apathy.
  4. Advanced language deficits, psychotic symptoms such as paranoia, motor deficits, and Parkinsonian-type symptoms appear.

If you’re a helping professional working with a younger person who plays collision sports, asking if they have experienced any of the above, most likely items in stage one or two, could be imperative to their future neurocognitive health. If they or their parent/guardian affirm the presence of symptoms, it does not mean they are developing CTE, as other factors could account for them. However, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, and further psychological/neurological evaluation could be the first step in stalling or perhaps even arresting the development of CTE.

Disclaimer: The material provided in this post is for informational purposes only and is not intended to diagnose, treat, or prevent any illness in readers or people they know. The information should not replace personalized care or intervention from an individual’s provider or formal supervision if you’re a practitioner or student.

item.title: Teaching Kids to Get Ahead of Their Anxiety By Expecting It
item.description:
Anxiety

Teaching Kids to Get Ahead of Their Anxiety By Expecting It

Simple strategies to navigate worry by shrinking and approaching kids' fears.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Teaching kids to expect worries helps them feel empowered to "test" worry, rather than "trust" it.
  • We can help kids separate from fears by asking, "what is worry saying to you," not, "why are you worried?"
  • Kids can learn to shrink their fears through fact-checking, right-size risk, and approach one step at a time.
Parents can help children navigate anxiety by explaining how it works
Source: FGTrade/iStock/ Used with permission

Welcome to a new school year!

As kids are settling into the rhythms of the new year, the fears they brought with them—“Will I have friends? Will the teacher be nice?” have quieted down, but likely others have popped in—the book report, the class camping trip, the cafeteria dynamics. When families experience what feels like a whack-a-mole dynamic with fears—resolve one, and another (or two or three) takes its place, it’s easy to think, “We’ll never get anywhere!” But that’s not how it has to be.

Expecting Anxiety Doesn’t Mean Expecting Your Child to Be Anxious

If we want kids to be equipped to navigate their emotions wherever they land, one thing we need to do is help them expect certain emotions to come up—what comes up most? Anxiety.

Fears and worries are normal and expected parts of life—but just waiting for them to pass is not our only option. Anxiety thrives on what is unfamiliar or uncertain. It sets off an alarm. By expecting fears and worries, we can teach kids what anxiety is and what to do next. When we help kids expect anxiety as a super-fast, no-fault worst-case scenario narrative that always gets there first, kids can be prepared when it shows up, not scared by what it’s telling them. They can learn that their job is to test worry, not trust it. Rather than feeling their only choices are being stuck stressing or avoiding, they can learn to unpack their fears, analyze instead of catastrophize. That’s what it means to get ahead of anxiety.

Where Do We Go From Here? Helping Your Child Understand Fear is How They’ll Really Feel Better

When our kids are upset, parents can feel hijacked at warp speed in an emergency-mode crossroads. We have to do something. Do we help our kids feel better by distracting, reassuring, or simply jumping right in and “fixing” situations for our kids fears on the one hand, or, “tough loving-it”: leave them to sink or swim so they will learn how to grow. When it comes to our kids’ emotional lives, it can feel like those two instincts are at odds.

Truly we don’t have to choose like that. When we do an inner pivot from: “How do I help my child feel better?” to “How do I help my child understand themselves better?” suddenly what feels like opposites, come together as collaborators: we are helping our kids feel better because they feel heard and understood by us, and they are now headed in a direction of growth because they are asking questions, and responding to our questions. They are separate from their fears and that shift in direction helps them have a shift in perspective: they are curious, deciders, interpreters, choosers, of understanding why they are feeling the way they are and what they can do about it often themselves to feel better.

Let the Unpacking Begin: Three Essential Shifts to Teaching Your Child to Navigate Anxiety

Separate Your Child from Their Fears and Help Them Name What They Are. When children feel overwhelmed with anxiety or, really any emotion—the feelings can overtake them and seem like an identity--that is permanently who they are instead of temporarily what they’re experiencing. “I am anxious” doesn’t mean “I’m feeling anxious.” Instead, it has come to mean: “I’m anxious; this is who I am, and that’s why I can’t do this hard thing.”

We need to help kids know that naming the emotion is the starting point, not the destination. The first step in order for all of that to happen is to separate themselves from their feelings and it is a simple edit that makes it happen.

A child says: “I’m so anxious!” Instead of responding with, “It’s OK, or what are you anxious about?” We can say: “I understand that you’re feeling anxiety, this is a new situation so there are a lot of unknowns. What is anxiety saying to you? What do you think?”

Suddenly they are on the outside of the anxiety looking in—as interpreters, questioners, analysts. Giving that anxious voice a name, “the Worry Bug, or Disaster Guy,” helps emphasize this separation. It turns what is vague and overwhelming into something concrete they can observe, edit, and increasingly take charge of.

How to Help Kids Unpack, Shrink and Rethink Fears. Once we know what anxiety is telling them, we want to encourage kids to put that to the test. Not putting your child to the test as in… “Why do you think that?” but empowering your child to put worry to the test: “What do you think of what worry is saying, does that sound likely to you or does it sound scary to you?”

As much as we might want to just correct our kids (lovingly) and say—“that’s not true, or that’s not going to happen!” it’s going to be more effective in the short run and the long run to teach them how to reach those conclusions themselves. Two strategies help kids gain the perspective—the first is “fact checking”—ask kids to pick up their “red pen” like the teacher would and correct what worry is saying to them. Is it a fear or a fact? Can you give worry a true false test? Or, asking the “million-dollar question” if they could win a million dollars by guessing right what will happen, would they bet on worry or on another idea.

Another strategy for fact-checking is getting a “second opinion” by bringing in their panel of experts, their inner board of directors—consulting their favorite athlete, celebrity, teacher—through their imagination. What would that role model say? And what do you think?

How to Help Kids Experiment with Approaching: Practice Makes Progress: Slow and Steady, and Rehearsals for the Win. Once kids have shrunk the fears down through their fact-checking, it’s time to take the show on the road because seeing is believing—no amount of talking can substitute for the experience of seeing that you can be afraid, and you can still do hard things, and the anxiety resolves—and you might even feel really proud of yourself. The key is finding the right-sized challenge: not too easy where they won’t feel a sense of accomplishment, but also not too hard where they aren’t likely to desensitize, they may feel like they need to leave midway, thus reinforcing the anxiety instead of their courage.

I like to teach about desensitization by talking about what it’s like to get into a cold swimming pool. How does it feel at first? Freezing! What happens after a few minutes? It feels better! Why is that? Because we adjust. Bingo. We are built to adjust. We need to hang in with an experience for a bit to see that we do adjust.

Practicing dry runs counts! Doing rehearsals and partial steps count! Remember, any “approaching” a feared situation leads to more useful information than avoiding does, so be flexible in acknowledging the challenges that miss the bullseye but land on the board.

May this be the year when more kids learn to navigate anxiety by expecting it so they can unpack it, dismantle its logic, and build up new experiences that unchecked anxiety would never let them have.

Here’s to a great school year and as always, here’s to less worry all around.
